children.text: A small volcanic island in the sea south of Dumaguete, where a marine protected area the residents have guarded themselves makes it almost certain you'll meet sea turtles in the shallows. It is a model case of Filipino community-based marine conservation and a world-class diving destination.
Apo Island is a small volcanic island rising from the sea about
7km
off the southeastern tip of Negros. It covers only about 0.74 km², measuring around
1.5km
north to south and
1km
east to west, and its highest point is about
above sea level. Its coastline runs about
4.5km
, with seven small beaches tucked between steep rocky cliffs. Administratively it is one barangay (village) of the city of Dauin in Negros Oriental, and according to the
census 920 residents live here by fishing and tourism. It has nothing to do with Mount Apo in Mindanao or
Apo Reef
off Mindoro, so take care not to confuse them when booking.
The island is famous less for the sea itself than for the way it has been protected. In the
, dynamite fishing and muro-ami (a method of pounding the coral to drive fish into nets) wrecked the reefs and catches kept shrinking. In

, the marine laboratory of Silliman University in Dumaguete proposed a sanctuary where fishing would be banned completely, and after long conversations between Dr. Angel Alcala and the residents, the fishermen themselves set aside about
of coastline and
out to sea as a no-fishing zone in
. In
, residents and the local council turned this into an ordinance to be managed by elected island residents, and on
August 9, 1994

, Presidential Proclamation No. 438 designated the island and about 691 hectares of surrounding sea as a protected landscape and seascape. It is the second-oldest community-based marine sanctuary in the Philippines, and there are reports that the weight of large predatory fish inside the no-take zone has grown eightfold.

Today more than 650 fish species and over 400 coral species have been recorded in Apo Island's waters, and the corals account for most of the roughly 450 species found in the Philippines. The biggest draw for travelers is the chance to see green and hawksbill sea turtles grazing on the shallow seagrass just off the beach from up close. Even weak swimmers can enjoy it in a life vest by following a village guide. These guides belong to an association the residents formally set up in
(ASIERGA); it has more than 300 members, who are said to have been trained in environmental law and in serving visitors. In
, a field officer of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) said that about 3,000 people visit the island each month.

It suits families who want to snorkel with turtles, experienced divers looking for current-swept walls and coral gardens, and travelers who want to stay on a quiet island in the afternoons after the day-trippers have left. Note, however, that electricity, water, and cell signal are limited, and on some days boats cannot run because of the weather.

In the shallow seagrass in front of the village, you meet grazing sea turtles almost every time. A village guide must accompany you in the turtle area, and under the guidelines you should stay at least
3m
away from the turtles and never touch or chase them. To protect the coral, fins are sometimes not allowed and you may be limited to a mask and life vest, so follow your guide's instructions.

Inside the island's sanctuary, leaf and plate corals and soft corals grow thickly, and you can see turtles, triggerfish, and parrotfish. Access is limited, and on some days only snorkeling is allowed, so book through a dive shop and follow the instructions on site that day.

At Chapel Point, a sand slope drops into a wall that falls past 30 m, with small caves and turtles to see. Coconut and Cogon Points have strong currents and are famous for drift diving, suited to intermediate and advanced divers, while the coral slopes at Rock Point East and West are full of frogfish and nudibranchs. The dive shop decides where to go by checking the current that day.
Starting behind Liberty's Lodge above the village, a steep climb up stairs and a dirt path takes
20–30 minutes
to reach the lighthouse near the top of the island. Climbing the ladder inside the lighthouse costs about
, and from the top you can see the main island of Negros and the sea in one sweep. There is nowhere to buy anything along the path, so bring water.

The island village has the sanctuary's management office, a school, and souvenir stalls. Part of the ecotourism income is said to go to the national government, with the rest used for managing the sanctuary and supporting village livelihoods, so buying T-shirts and handicrafts made by the residents helps.

blocks.title: Spending a night on the island

children.text: Once the day-tour boats leave in the afternoon, the island becomes surprisingly quiet. You can watch the sun set over the western sea, see stars in a sky with few lights, and in the early morning meet turtles on an empty beach.

In Malatapay, where the boats depart, a market is held every Wednesday, trading livestock such as cattle, pigs, and goats and selling roast whole pig (lechon) by the kilogram. There are also many seafood and fruit stalls, so it is a good place to look around in the morning before boarding your boat.

Staying on the island gives you quiet mornings and evenings, but if the weather turns, your return can be delayed, so leave a spare day in your return schedule.
Cebu Pacific and PAL Express, a Philippine Airlines affiliate, fly nonstop from Manila to Dumaguete (Sibulan Airport, DGT), taking about
1 hour 20 minutes
. The airport lies about
3–5km
north of downtown Dumaguete, around 15 minutes by tricycle. The Apo Island boats leave from Malatapay, about
south of the airport, so on your arrival day it is more relaxed to spend the night in Dumaguete or Dauin and head to the island the next morning.
At the Dumaguete southern terminal or along the road, take a bus or jeepney bound for Zamboanguita, Bais, or Bayawan and ask to be dropped off at Malatapay. It takes about
40 minutes–1 hour
, and the one-way fare by bus or jeepney is about
. After getting off at the roadside, it is a
5–10 minutes
walk along the market road to the pier. If you tell the driver or conductor in advance that you are going to "Apo Island," they will let you know where to get off.

The OceanJet fast ferry from Cebu via Tagbilaran, Bohol to Dumaguete takes about
4 hours 20 minutes
, with fares listed at about
. However, in
there were periods when service was reduced or suspended because of fuel costs, so check the official announcements before you leave.
We could not confirm any scheduled boat that goes from Siquijor straight to Apo Island, so you go through Dumaguete. The Siquijor–Dumaguete OceanJet fast ferry takes about
50 minutes–1 hour
, and fares vary by source, at around
. In the spring of
some trips were suspended, so check the timetable, and it is safer to stay in Dumaguete and head to Malatapay in the morning.
Your trip to Apo Island varies a great deal with the waves. Travel guides generally treat
November–May
as the good season, and many of the days with the best visibility fall in
March–June
, when the sea is calmest and the water warmest. From
December–February
the northeast monsoon (amihan) blows and waves can rise in the afternoon, but travel is generally possible.
From
July–October

, the southwest monsoon (habagat) and typhoons mean more days when bangka trips are canceled and the sea turns rough. In any season, the rule is to cross early in the morning and return in the early afternoon, since the waves often rise in the afternoon. The water temperature is generally
all year, so a thin rash guard is enough for snorkeling.

Most travelers stay in downtown Dumaguete or at a Dauin coastal resort and visit as a day trip. Dauin has a string of dive resorts, such as Atlantis Dive Resort and Mike's Dauin Beach Resort, that run their own Apo Island boats, making an early departure easy. On the island there are small lodgings such as Liberty's Lodge, Apo Island Beach Resort, and Mario's Homestay; many cost about
per night and include meals, and dorm beds are said to start at about
. Rooms are few, so book ahead in the high season.

Electricity on the island comes from generators and is supplied only at set hours, and rooms without air conditioning are the norm. Water is collected rain, and many places wash with a large bucket; Wi-Fi is available only at some lodgings. Meals are taken at your lodging's restaurant or a small village eatery and center on simple home cooking such as grilled fish, stir-fried vegetables, and rice. The lechon and grilled seafood at the Wednesday market in Malatapay on the main island are local specialties, so be sure to try them if your schedule allows.
There are no ATMs on the island and cards are rarely accepted, so bring plenty of cash for entrance fees, guide fees, and meals.
Cell signal reaches only parts of the island. Confirm lodging reservations and arrangements with your bangka driver on the mainland beforehand.
Although we could not confirm it as an official rule, it is better to cover your skin with a rash guard and long leggings rather than chemical sunscreen, for the sake of the coral.
The turtle area is crowded around
2 p.m.

, when the day-tour boats arrive. It is quieter right after you arrive, in the late afternoon, and at dawn the next day if you stay overnight; the times when many turtles come also vary with the tide, so ask your guide.
The island has no pier, so you step off into knee-deep water. Wear aqua shoes or waterproof sandals, and keep your passport and electronics in a waterproof bag.
When photographing with a waterproof camera, turn off the flash and shoot from above at a downward angle so you don't disturb the turtles.
If you get seasick badly, take motion-sickness medicine
30 minutes
before boarding the bangka and sit in the middle of the back of the boat. You may get wet from splashing waves.
If you are a weak swimmer, wear a life vest and stay close to the guide. Even where it looks shallow, there is current beyond the edge.
If you are staying overnight on the island, bring a headlamp, a power bank, insect repellent, and water, and charge your devices when the electricity is on.
Touching, chasing, or riding turtles and stepping on coral are strictly prohibited, and you may be fined or expelled from the island.
In strong-current spots such as Coconut and Cogon Points, snorkelers can be swept away. Enter the water only in areas the guide permits.

Waves tend to rise in the afternoon, so if the bangka driver suggests returning earlier, follow his advice. There are also days when the coast guard stops departures, so leave yourself some slack on the day you return.
Entrance, snorkeling, and diver fees are set by the sanctuary's management board, and as of
there are reports that they are under review and concerns about increases. Check the latest announcements before you leave.
It is a small island, so you have to go back to the main island for proper medical care. Disinfect coral scrapes right away and check them again after you return.
Jellyfish and sea urchins can sting, so do not walk barefoot across shallow rocky areas.
Apo Island (Negros) has a name similar to Mount Apo in Mindanao and Apo Reef near Coron. Confirm the location when you book a dive.

by car to Malatapay. A gentle city famous for its seaside promenade, university district, and desserts, and the base for an Apo Island trip.

From Dumaguete's Sibulan port it is about

by boat to Liloan port, and then you still have to travel overland. It is famous for whale shark watching, and fitting it into the same day is a tight squeeze.
